en: The Sūtra on the Simile of the Arrow, spoken by the Buddha;
the name of the translator is lost, and it is now appended to the Record of the Eastern Jin.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, while the Venerable Mālukyaputta was staying alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in him:

"The Blessed One has abandoned wrong views and eliminated wrong views; yet he does not declare or explain whether the world is eternal or non-eternal, whether the world is finite or infinite, whether the life-principle is the same as the body or the life-principle is different from the body, whether there is an afterlife or no afterlife, or whether there both is and is not an afterlife."
"I cannot endure it; it is not what I accept, nor what I delight in.
World-Honored One, if you were to categorically declare that the world is eternal, I would follow you and practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
If the World-Honored One does not categorically declare that the world is eternal, then having finished this discussion, I shall depart."

Thus regarding the world: whether the world is finite, or the world is infinite; whether the life-principle is the same as the body, or the life-principle is different from the body; whether there is an end to this life, or there is no end to this life; whether this exists, or this does not exist; whether there is an end to existence, or there is no end to existence.
"If the Blessed One were to categorically declare to me that 'this alone is the truth and all else is delusion,' then I would practice the holy life.
If the Blessed One does not categorically declare to me that 'this alone is the truth and all else is delusion,' then having asked my question, I shall depart."

Thereupon, the Venerable Mālukyaputta rose from his seat in the late afternoon, went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arrival, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Having sat down to one side, the Venerable Mālukyaputta addressed the Blessed One, saying: “Blessed One,
while I was in seclusion, this thought arose in me:”

"I say this: that the Blessed One, having abandoned false views and eliminated false views, does not declare or teach that the world is eternal, nor even that there is no life after death—this I do not desire, I cannot endure, and I do not find it pleasing."
If the Blessed One definitively knows that the world is eternal, the Blessed One should declare it;
if the Blessed One definitively does not know that the world is eternal, he should simply state directly, "I cannot know it."

"Thus, regarding the world's impermanence up to its lack of a life-principle at death, if the Blessed One knows for certain that my words are the truth and others are foolish, the Blessed One should declare it;
if the Blessed One does not know whether my words are the truth and others are foolish, he should simply say, 'I do not know.'"
“Mālukyaputta! Did I ever say to you before:
‘If I were to declare that the world is eternal, would you then follow me and practice the holy life’?”
"No, indeed, World-Honored One!

If it were the case that this world is impermanent up to its final passing away, and if I were to declare: 'My words are the absolute truth, while all else is foolishness,' would you then follow me and practice the holy life?"
"No, indeed, World-Honored One! You,
Mālukyaputta, previously spoke these words to me:..."
“If the Blessed One were to categorically declare that the world is eternal, would I then follow him and practice the holy life? “No,
indeed, World-Honored One.”

“If it is thus that the world is impermanent up to the point of having no life at its end, and if the Blessed One were to declare to me: ‘This alone is the truth; all else is delusion,’ would I then practice the holy life under him?”
"No, indeed, World-Honored One! This is Mālakumāra!"
“I never spoke to you before, nor did you ever speak to me before!
You foolish man, why do you revile me without cause?
Thereupon, the Venerable Mālukyaputta, having been rebuked by the Blessed One, remained silent; sweat broke out on his face and body, and he turned his head away, speechless and silent.
At that time, having rebuked Māra Kumāra face to face, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If there were a foolish person who thought thus:
'I will not practice the holy life under the Blessed One until the Blessed One definitively declares that the world is eternal.'"
"That foolish person does not realize that he will meet his end in the interim.

'In this way, while the world is impermanent and subject to death, I shall not practice the holy life under the Blessed One; I must first compel the Blessed One to declare that my words are the truth and all others are foolish.'"
That person does not realize that they have passed away midway.

It is like someone whose body has been struck by a poisoned arrow; their relatives, out of compassion for them, wishing to bring them peace and wishing to benefit them, seek out a physician to extract the poisoned arrow.
Then that person thinks to himself:

"I will not remove this arrow until I know the person who struck me—his clan, his name, and his appearance; whether he is tall, short, or of medium height; whether he is dark or fair; whether he is of the Kṣatriya caste, the Brāhmaṇa caste, the Vaiśya caste, or the Śūdra caste; and who among those from the east, south, west, or north has struck me with this arrow?"
Without removing this poisoned arrow, I must first know whether that bow is made of sāla wood, tāla wood, or of khadira or aṅgīrī wood.
Without removing this poisoned arrow, I must first know its sinew: whether it is cow-sinew, sheep-sinew, or yak-sinew used to wrap that bow?
"I will not extract this poisoned arrow until I know whether its grip is made of white bone, black lacquer, or red lacquer;
I will not extract this poisoned arrow until I know whether its string is made of cow sinew, sheep sinew, or yak sinew."
"I will not remove this poisoned arrow until I know whether that shaft is made of śāla wood, or of bamboo, or of rāyagiḷa wood."
I will not remove this poisoned arrow until I know whether the sinew used to wrap the shaft is from an ox, a sheep, or a yak.
I will not remove this poisoned arrow until I know whether its feathers are those of a peacock, a crane, or a vulture, and from which wings they were taken to serve as plumes.
I will not remove this poisoned arrow until I know whether that iron shaft is made of *vaca*, *bala*, *nara*, or *kāla*.

"I will not remove this poisoned arrow until I know that smith’s clan name, his personal name, his physical appearance, whether he is tall, short, or of medium height, whether he is black or white, and whether he lives in the east, the south, the west, or the north."
"That person would likewise be unable to know it, for he would pass away midway.
In the same way, if there were a foolish person who thought:
'I will not practice the holy life under that Blessed One unless the Blessed One declares that the world is eternal.'"
That foolish person, unaware of this, shall meet his end in the interim.
Thus, the world is not eternal; the world has limits, up until the point where life comes to an end.
If there is a foolish person who thinks:
"I will not practice the holy life under that Blessed One; rather, I shall compel the Blessed One to declare of me: 'This one speaks the truth, all others are fools.'"
That foolish person, unaware of this, shall meet his end in the interim.
Holding the false view that "the world is eternal," he will likewise practice the holy life under me.
If one holds the wrong view that "the world is impermanent" up to "there is no life after death," such a person should nevertheless practice the holy life under me.
However, if one holds the wrong view that "the world is eternal," they should not follow me in practicing the holy life.
Thus, regarding the view that the world is impermanent up to the point of having no life after death—if one holds such a wrong view, one should not follow me in practicing the holy life.
However, if one holds the view that the world is eternal, being free from such a wrong view, then one should indeed follow me in practicing the holy life.
In this way, for those who hold the wrong view that the world is impermanent up to the point of having no life after death, they should follow my practice of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
For those who hold the wrong view that the world is eternal, they should not follow my practice of the holy life.
Thus, regarding the world as impermanent up to its being without a life-span, one who holds such wrong view should not practice the holy life under me.
[But] the world is permanent; there is birth, aging, sickness, and death, and there is sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress; thus this great mass of suffering has its origin.
Thus, regarding the world as impermanent up to its being without life at the end, that there is birth and aging, up to this mass of great suffering—this is the way things are.
To say "the world is eternal" is not to be declared;
likewise, to say "the world is impermanent up to its being without life at the end" is not to be declared.
Why is it undeclared?

Because this is neither the true meaning, nor the Dharma, nor the holy life; it does not accomplish supernormal powers, does not lead to the equal path, and is not associated with Nirvana. Therefore, it is undeclared.
What is that which I categorically declare? I categorically declare:
"This is suffering. I categorically declare:
"The origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the way leading to the cessation of suffering."

Why is this? I have given a categorical declaration that this is the meaning, this is the Dharma; it leads to the attainment of supernormal powers, the practice of the holy life, the realization of the equal path, and is in accordance with Nirvana. For this reason, I have declared it categorically.
"What is not to be recorded should be abandoned; what is recorded by me should be upheld.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the World-Honored One had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and were delighted.
The Sūtra on the Simile of the Arrow Spoken by the Buddha
